narrative:
The model estimated a 52.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means the prediction was only slightly more likely to be failure than success, but it was enough for your application to be denied under the school’s process. The denial was not based on gender or race.

The most influential factor was your part-time enrollment status, which pushed the prediction toward failure. Among accepted students, 92.8% were full-time and only 7.2% were part-time, so your profile differs sharply from the group the school typically admits. The second most important factor was your LSAT score, which leaned toward passing in your individual assessment; your score was 34, compared with an accepted-student average of 37.18. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor and also leaned toward passing; at 3.30 it was slightly above the accepted average of 3.23. Even so, the part-time factor was stronger than the two factors favoring success, leaving the final prediction just above the failure threshold.

You should ask admissions for feedback, especially whether moving to full-time study or documenting why part-time study is necessary would change the assessment. Consider retaking the LSAT or strengthening your academic record, then reapply when you can address the part-time issue directly.
